title: Down the Rabbit Hole
author: Lippert, Samantha
summary: Samantha Lippert describes how a single striking data point — a 40-67% special education identification rate in one district — drew her into a system-level investigation of why so many students were being classified, what that classification was delivering for them, and why intervention feedback loops were broken. The article is a first-person account of discovering that the identification process was functioning as a referral pipeline rather than a precision diagnostic instrument, driven by overwhelmed classroom teachers with no other tools and a compliance infrastructure that rewarded documentation over outcomes. Lippert documents the gap between what IDEA promises and what the identification process actually delivers, particularly in under-resourced districts. She traces over-identification to teacher capacity gaps, inadequate general-education intervention tiers, and the path-of-least-resistance logic of formal referral. The piece ends with a call for honest institutional reckoning about what the identification system is actually accomplishing versus what it was designed to do.
points: A 40-67% special education identification rate in one district is not a clinical finding — it is a system finding about the state of general education.
The IDEA identification process, under pressure, functions as a referral pipeline rather than a precision diagnostic instrument calibrated to actual student need.
Over-identification is not an error in the system — it is the rational output of a system where the general education tier lacks the capacity to intervene.
Compliance infrastructure around IEPs rewards documentation over outcomes, consuming staff capacity that could otherwise be deployed directly with students.
Honest reckoning with identification rates requires asking what the system is actually accomplishing, not only what it was originally designed to accomplish.
quotes: Of my 12 general education students in my class this past year, I had 9 students all land at a Level P for their running record, but because my class also administers Oral Reading Fluency measures, I am able to see clear discrepancy between the two different data points.

That means building a collaborative meeting structure in which grade-level teams and interventionists actually look at student response together — often enough that an ineffective intervention can be changed before another benchmark window arrives.

When that class with 12 identified students gets to 3rd grade, assuming nothing changes before then and now and our SPED model remains the same, my co-taught class will have a SPED rate of 67% based on the expected class size for that cohort.

My team plans to use Acadience again next year, and after seeing and sharing our data with other teachers this year, there are several other teachers who plan to also implement this assessment on their own with their students next year.

If classroom teachers don’t know where the information lives, don’t routinely receive their own students’ results, and don’t use those results when intervention and instructional decisions are made, the problem isn’t data collection.

The question I’m asking is at the cohort level: When unusually large proportions of successive cohorts require specialized services, should we also be examining what happened instructionally before those students reached that point?

I would then move towards focusing more attention on K–1 instruction because that’s where we have the best chance to intervene before the gaps become severe, while obviously continuing support for older students who already need it.
